paragraphs: Touch typing is a skill of the hands, not of the eyes. The fingers rest on the home row and know the way to every key. After each press the finger comes back, so the next move always starts from the same point. That is why you never need to look down: the hand already knows where it is.

A pianist does not begin with a concert. First come the scales: short, simple and always the same. They may seem dull, yet they teach the fingers to move evenly and exactly. Typing works the same way. Short repeated drills build the move, and later those moves turn into words, lines and whole pages.

Speed cannot be taken by force. When you rush, the fingers get mixed up, and each mistake costs more time than the hurry ever saved. It is far better to type a little slower but evenly, without stops. Once accuracy becomes a habit, the pace grows on its own and needs no pushing.

In the morning a mist lay over the river. The fisherman sat on the bank and did not hurry, because fish do not like fuss. Somewhere far away a car passed, a dog barked, and it was quiet again. The sun rose above the forest, the mist was gone, and the water looked like a large calm mirror.

Every town has its own old street. The houses are low, the pavements are narrow, and the trees remember more than the people do. By day it is busy with shops and small cafes, and in the evening the yellow lamps come on and the street looks the way it did a hundred years ago.

A good habit grows slowly. In the first week it takes effort, in the second it takes reminders, and after a month it is simply part of the day. Twenty minutes of typing a day looks small, yet over a year it adds up to more than a hundred hours of practice. No single long session can match that.
